questions.title: Transport layer
questions.text: Describe **two** functions of the transport layer.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): splits data into segments; adds port numbers so data reaches the right application; sequence numbers / correct order; error control / acknowledgements; retransmission of lost segments; flow control
scheme.model_answer: It splits data into segments with port numbers so the data reaches the right application, and it checks that all segments arrive, resending any that are lost.

questions.title: Data link layer
questions.text: Describe the role of the data link layer.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): organises bits into frames; adds source / destination MAC addresses; error detection on one link (trailer / checksum); controls access to the medium; used by switches / NICs
scheme.model_answer: It packs the data into frames with source and destination MAC addresses and adds a checksum so errors on the link can be detected.

questions.title: Encapsulation
questions.text: Explain what is meant by **encapsulation** in the OSI model.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- As data moves down the layers each layer adds its own header (data link also a trailer) with control information (1)
- the receiver removes the headers in reverse order as data moves up (decapsulation) (1)
scheme.model_answer: On the way down each layer wraps the data in its own header (and the data link layer adds a trailer); at the receiver each layer removes its header on the way up.

questions.title: OSI and TCP/IP
questions.text: Compare the OSI model with the TCP/IP model.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): OSI 7 layers vs TCP/IP 4; OSI is a reference / theoretical model vs TCP/IP is used in practice on the Internet; TCP/IP combines application, presentation and session into one application layer; TCP/IP combines data link and physical into network access
scheme.model_answer: OSI has seven layers and is a reference model, whereas TCP/IP has four layers and is the model the Internet actually uses; TCP/IP joins OSI's application, presentation and session layers into one application layer.

questions.title: The seven layers
questions.text: The OSI model divides network communication into seven layers.

scheme.mark_scheme: Presentation (1); Network (1); Data link (1)

Application: network services / protocols for applications, e.g. HTTP, SMTP (1). Presentation: encryption / compression / format conversion (1). Transport: segments, ports, reliable end-to-end delivery, retransmission (1). Network: logical (IP) addressing and routing of packets (1)
scheme.model_answer: Application: provides services such as HTTP to programs. Presentation: encrypts and compresses data. Transport: splits data into segments and resends lost ones. Network: routes packets using IP addresses.

questions.title: Sending a web request
questions.text: A student opens https://www.nis.edu.kz in a browser. The request passes down the OSI layers of the student's computer.

parts.title: Encapsulation
parts.text: Describe what happens to the request at the transport, network, data link and physical layers.

scheme.mark_scheme: Transport: split into segments, port number 443 / sequence numbers added (1); Network: IP addresses added → packets, routed (1); Data link: MAC addresses + trailer → frames (1); Physical: sent as bits / signals (1)
scheme.model_answer: Transport: TCP splits the request into segments with port 443 and sequence numbers. Network: IP adds source and destination IP addresses to make packets. Data link: MAC addresses and a checksum trailer are added to make frames. Physical: the frames are sent as electrical or radio signals.

parts.title: HTTPS
parts.text: Identify the layer where the request is encrypted and explain why this is needed.

scheme.mark_scheme: Presentation layer (1); so data cannot be read if intercepted / keeps passwords private (1)
scheme.model_answer: The presentation layer encrypts it so that anyone intercepting the data cannot read it.

parts.title: Receiver
parts.text: Describe what happens to the data when it reaches the web server.

scheme.mark_scheme: Data passes up the layers in reverse order (1); each layer removes its header / decapsulation until the request reaches the web server application (1)
scheme.model_answer: It goes up the server's layers from physical to application, and each layer removes its own header until the HTTP request reaches the web server software.

questions.title: Layered models
questions.text: Network designers use layered models such as OSI and TCP/IP.

parts.title: Benefits
parts.text: Explain **two** benefits of using a layered model.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): independent development / changes per layer; interoperability via standards; easier troubleshooting; complex problem divided into smaller parts
scheme.model_answer: 1 One layer can be changed (e.g. cable to Wi-Fi) without changing the others. 2 Faults are easier to find because they can be located in one layer.

parts.title: TCP/IP mapping
parts.text: Complete the TCP/IP layer that matches each OSI layer. Choose from **Application, Transport, Internet, Network access**.

scheme.mark_scheme: Application; Internet; Network access (1 each)

parts.title: Devices
parts.text: Explain why a router is said to work at a higher OSI layer than a switch.

scheme.mark_scheme: Router works at the network layer (3) using IP addresses to route between networks (1); switch works at the data link layer (2) using MAC addresses within a LAN (1)
scheme.model_answer: A router reads IP addresses and routes packets between networks (layer 3), while a switch only reads MAC addresses to forward frames inside one LAN (layer 2).

summary: The seven layers of the OSI reference model — the function of each layer, its data unit, typical protocols and devices — how data is encapsulated and decapsulated on its way through the layers, a worked example of a web request, the TCP/IP model compared with OSI, and the benefits of a layered model.

blocks.content: A **reference model with seven layers**, published by the ISO, that describes how data is sent from one device to another across a network. Each layer has a **specific function**, **provides services to the layer above** and **uses the services of the layer below**, so that hardware and software from different manufacturers can work together.

blocks.title: The seven layers (from top to bottom)
rows: Network services for user applications; the interface between the user's program and the network
HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP3, IMAP, DNS
SSL/TLS encryption, JPEG, MP3, ASCII / Unicode
Opens, manages and **closes sessions** (connections) between applications; synchronisation and checkpoints
**End-to-end** delivery between programs; splits data into **segments**, numbers them, error and flow control, retransmission
**Logical addressing** (IP addresses) and **routing** of **packets** between networks
**Physical (MAC) addressing**, organising bits into **frames**, error detection on one link, access to the medium
Transmits raw **bits** as electrical, light or radio signals; cables, connectors, voltages, frequencies

blocks.content: From layer **7 down**: "**A**ll **P**eople **S**eem **T**o **N**eed **D**ata **P**rocessing" — Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data link, Physical. From layer **1 up**: "**P**lease **D**o **N**ot **T**hrow **S**ausage **P**izza **A**way".

items.title: Upper layers (7–5) — "the software"
items.content:
- Deal with the **meaning** of the data for the user's application.
- Implemented in **software** on the end devices.

items.title: Transport layer (4) — "the link between"
items.content: - Makes sure the data from one **program** reaches the right **program** on the other device, complete and in order.

items.title: Lower layers (3–1) — "the network"
items.content:
- Move the data **across the network**: routing, local delivery, signals.
- Implemented in network **hardware** and drivers.

items.title: 7 Application layer
items.content:
- Provides **network services** to applications: web browsing (HTTP), e-mail (SMTP, POP3, IMAP), file transfer (FTP), name lookup (DNS).
- It is **not** the application itself (the browser) but the protocols the application uses.

items.title: 6 Presentation layer
items.content:
- Makes data understandable to the receiver: **converts formats** (character codes, image and video formats).
- **Encrypts** and **decrypts** data (TLS in HTTPS) and **compresses** it.

items.title: 5 Session layer
items.content:
- **Establishes, maintains and ends** a session (dialogue) between two applications.
- Adds **checkpoints**, so a long transfer can restart from the last checkpoint instead of from the beginning.

items.title: 4 Transport layer
items.content:
- Splits data into **segments** and adds **port numbers** so the data reaches the right application.
- **TCP**: reliable — acknowledgements, retransmission of lost segments, correct order, flow control. **UDP**: fast, no checks (video calls, games).

items.title: 3 Network layer
items.content:
- Adds **source and destination IP addresses** → **packets**.
- **Routers** choose the **best route** between networks.

items.title: 2 Data link layer
items.content:
- Adds **source and destination MAC addresses** and an error-checking **trailer** → **frames**.
- Controls access to the shared medium; **switches** forward frames inside a LAN.

items.title: 1 Physical layer
items.content:
- Converts frames into **bits** and sends them as **signals** — voltages on copper, light pulses in fibre, radio waves.
- Defines cables, connectors, pin layouts and transmission speed.

blocks.content: As data moves **down** the layers of the sender, each layer **adds its own header** (the data link layer also adds a **trailer**) containing the control information it needs. At the receiver, the data moves **up** the layers and each layer **removes** its header — **decapsulation**.

Application / Presentation / Session:                          [ DATA ]
Transport (segment):                                 [TCP header][ DATA ]
Network (packet):                          [IP header][TCP header][ DATA ]
Data link (frame):           [MAC header][IP header][TCP header][ DATA ][trailer]
Physical:                    0110100101010111010010110100101001011101010…
blocks.caption: Encapsulation going down the layers

blocks.content: Each layer communicates **logically** with the **same layer** on the other device: the transport layer of the sender talks to the transport layer of the receiver through the TCP header, while physically the data goes down to layer 1, across the medium and back up.

blocks.title: Example — a browser requests a web page
items: **7 Application**: the browser creates an **HTTP GET** request for `/index.html`.
**6 Presentation**: the request is **encrypted** with TLS (HTTPS) and encoded as text.
**5 Session**: a **session** with the web server is opened and kept for the following requests.
**4 Transport**: TCP splits the data into **segments**, adds **port 443** and sequence numbers.
**3 Network**: IP adds the source and destination **IP addresses** → **packets**; routers forward them.
**2 Data link**: Ethernet / Wi-Fi adds the **MAC address** of the next device (the router) and a checksum → **frames**.
**1 Physical**: the frames are sent as **electrical or radio signals**.
At the server the layers work **in reverse**: bits → frames → packets → segments → the HTTP request is given to the web server software.

blocks.title: Where common problems occur
rows: Unplugged or damaged cable, weak Wi-Fi signal
Switch port fault, MAC address conflict
Wrong IP address, router down, no route
Port blocked by a firewall, lost segments
Wrong URL, DNS error, web server error 404

blocks.title: OSI model vs TCP/IP model
rows: HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP3, DNS

items.title: OSI model
items.content:
- **7** layers; a **reference / teaching** model.
- Separates presentation and session clearly.
- Designed before the protocols — general.

items.title: TCP/IP model
items.content:
- **4** layers; the **practical** model the Internet actually uses.
- Upper three OSI layers are combined into one application layer.
- Designed around existing protocols (TCP and IP).

items.title: Benefits of a layered model
items.content:
- Each layer can be **designed, changed and tested independently** — e.g. Wi-Fi replaced Ethernet cable without changing HTTP.
- **Standards** let equipment and software from **different manufacturers** work together.
- Easier **troubleshooting** — a problem can be located in one layer.
- Easier to **learn and teach** networking; complex communication is broken into smaller tasks.

items.title: Drawbacks
items.content:
- Extra **headers** at each layer add overhead (more data to send).
- Some functions are **repeated** in several layers (e.g. error checking).

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Name the OSI layer that uses IP addresses. [1]**
**Network layer** (layer 3) (1).

**Q: Describe the functions of the transport layer. [2]**
Splits data into **segments** and adds **port numbers** / sequence numbers (1); ensures **reliable end-to-end delivery** — error checking, retransmission of lost segments, correct order (1).

**Q: State the layer responsible for encryption and data compression. [1]**
**Presentation layer** (1).

**Q: Explain what is meant by encapsulation. [2]**
Each layer **adds a header** (and the data link layer a trailer) with its control information as data passes **down** the layers (1); the receiver **removes** them in reverse order as data passes **up** (1).

- Putting the layers in the wrong order — Physical is layer **1**, Application layer **7**.
- Saying the application layer **is** the browser — it is the **protocols** used by the application.
- Mixing up **IP** (network layer, routers) and **MAC** (data link layer, switches).
- Calling a layer-2 unit a "packet" — it is a **frame**; layer 4 is a **segment**.
